Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety

which anxiety, and how to treatAre the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Exclude a cause first: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) glucose urine toxicology; consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) for palpitations or chest pain
  • Recurrent unexpected attacks 1 month or more of worry or behavior change panic disorder; no test makes the diagnosis
  • CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both; start the drug low, raise slowly; benzodiazepine short term only
What it is

Recurrent unexpected attacks worry about more of them or avoidance of their triggers

Attack: abrupt surge of fear The attackTypically lasts 5 to 20 minutes; often unexpected, and some attacks wake the person from sleep. 4 or more of 13 symptoms

Driver

Proposed: catastrophic reading of normal body sensations

Triggers

Affected first-degree relative non-modifiable female sex: about twice as often as in men non-modifiable

Anxious temperament stressful life events

Chain

Proposed: body sensation appraised as catastrophic fear peaks within minutes

Worry about the next attack AvoidanceAvoidance includes situations that mimic an attack, such as exercise, caffeine or spicy foods.

Insights

Attacks occur in other anxiety disorders too: ask what the fear is about

Lactate can provoke attacks in panic disorder more often than in healthy people, but with no standardized criteria it is a known finding, not a diagnostic test

Who, mechanism and coursedetail behind the chain
WhoUsually starts in late adolescence or early adulthood; uncommon before age 14; women affected about twice as often as men
FamilyRaised risk in first-degree relatives
MechanismProposed: oversensitive carbon dioxide detectors in the medulla, leading to breathing changes and hypocapnia (↓ blood carbon dioxide)Sodium lactate, carbon dioxide, caffeine and yohimbine can provoke attacks more often in people with panic disorder than in healthy controls
CourseMost relapse even after a symptom-free period; only about 60% remit within 6 months
2Urgent risks
HeartPalpitations or chest pain
Regular, abrupt on and off: SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) may be misread as panic

If palpitations or chest pain occur, choose an ECG. Guideline detailPalpitations: preexcitation or a short or long QT (Q wave to T wave) interval; chest pain: ischemia, infarction or pericarditis

Blood pressureSevere hypertension during the episodes

If the blood pressure is severely high in a spell, choose plasma free metanephrines.

SubstanceStimulant or cannabis intoxication, or alcohol withdrawal, can precipitate attacks

If attacks occur only during intoxication or withdrawal from the substance, choose substance-induced attacks, not panic disorder.

SuicidePanic disorder raises the risk of depression, suicidal ideation, and alcohol and substance use

If panic disorder is diagnosed, choose asking about suicidal ideation, depression and substance use.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected attacks peaking within minutes1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a behavior change
AgoraphobiaAvoids crowds, lines, public transportation, open or enclosed places, or being out aloneEscape hard or help unavailable, in 2 or more of 5 situations; typically 6 months or more; with panic disorder, give both
Social anxiety disorder (social phobia)Attacks only in social situations with possible scrutinyFear of negative evaluation, not of the attacks; typically 6 months or more
Specific phobiaAttacks only with one feared triggerOne object or situation, almost always immediate fear; not the 2 or more of 5 agoraphobia situations; typically 6 months or more Past traumaA past trauma linked to the feared thing is not PTSD (posttraumatic stress disorder) without intrusive symptoms such as flashbacks or nightmares, pervasive hyperarousal, or negative thoughts about the event.
Generalized anxiety disorderIn primary careOften presents in primary care with fatigue, muscle tension with pain (headache; neck, shoulder or back pain), insomnia, trembling, sweating or gastrointestinal symptoms; chronic, often lifelong, worse in stress. The worry spans everyday issues; in somatic symptom disorder the anxiety centers on the symptoms and the fear of serious illness. Patients may repeat tasks and seek reassurance.At least 6 months, more days than not; 3 or more of 6 symptoms (1 in children) Against panic and depressionGeneralized anxiety disorder does not feature unexpected attacks; chronic anxiety in panic disorder is fear of the next attack. Generalized anxiety disorder and panic disorder can coincide; then both diagnoses are given. Depression can bring anxiety, fatigue and insomnia too, but needs persistent low mood or anhedonia.
(hypochondriasis)Preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness; mild or no symptomsAt least 6 months; persistent, while panic is typically acute and episodic
Distressing body symptoms with disproportionate thoughts, high health anxiety or excessive time spentTypically more than 6 months symptomatic; panic anxiety is typically acute and episodic
Weight loss, heat intolerance, resting tachycardia, tremor↓ TSH, ↑ free thyroxine
Stimulant or cannabis intoxication; withdrawal from a depressant such as alcohol or a barbiturateAttacks only during intoxication or withdrawal from the substance; history and urine toxicology
Episodic headache, sweating, racing heartSevere hypertension in the episodes; ↑ plasma free metanephrines
SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) or another arrhythmiaRegular fast palpitations; abrupt start, abrupt stopRegular, abrupt on and off; ECG ideally during an episode; Holter or event monitoring may be needed
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Weight loss, heat intolerance, resting tachycardiaHyperthyroidismTSH; ↑ free thyroxine confirms
Severe hypertension with headache and sweating in spellsPheochromocytomaPlasma free metanephrines
Palpitations that start and stop abruptly, regular and fastSVT or preexcitationECG before calling them panic attacks
Attacks when speaking to an audience and also unexpectedly at homePanic disorder, not social anxietyDiagnose panic disorder if worry about more attacks lasts 1 month or more
Pause point
Suspected panic disorder Offered: a lactate challenge to confirm it The optionsAbnormal eye tracking: “going crazy” suggests psychosis; but abnormal eye tracking goes with schizophrenia, and patients with panic disorder do not show it.
Delayed rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on polysomnography: the stem mentions sleep; but it can be found in sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder and with some drugs and alcohol; no known association exists with panic disorder.
Enlarged third and lateral ventricles on head CT (computed tomography): a structural brain cause; but that pattern comes from aqueductal stenosis, the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus, which is atypical in a healthy young adult and does not explain the attacks.
Cortisol not suppressed by 1 mg of dexamethasone: a stress-axis test; but nonsuppression points to Cushing syndrome, not panic disorder.
Down to two: increased sensitivity to lactate infusions or cortisol nonsuppression. Lactate: recurrent attacks that come out of the blue, with a normal workup, point to panic disorder (the NBME answer), and patients with it have attacks in response to lactate at an increased rate (NBME ties this to catastrophic appraisal of body states). Its diagnostic utility is unclear: there are no standardized criteria. The stem never states worry or avoidance, and the lead-in asks for a finding, not the diagnosis. No test confirms it; lactate challenges lack standardized criteria → No confirmatory test

But when the question asks which abnormality the patient most likely has, increased sensitivity to lactate is the answer.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: panic disorder Attacks – recurrent unexpected panic attacks; each an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort, peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms (STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's) · Aftermath – at least 1 month, after at least 1 attack, of persistent worry about more attacks or their consequences, or a significant maladaptive behavior change, such as avoidance, tied to the attacks · Cause – not attributable to a substance or another medical condition · Other – not better explained by another mental disorder
STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's
  • S – sweating
  • T – trembling
  • U – unsteadiness, dizziness
  • D – depersonalization, derealization
  • E – excessive heart rate, palpitations
  • N – nausea or abdominal distress
  • T – tingling
  • S – shortness of breath
  • FEAR – of dying; of losing control or going crazy
  • C – chest pain, chills or heat sensations, choking
7Treatment
1

1st lineat diagnosis

CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or SSRI or SNRIAn SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor). Typically reserved for an inadequate SSRI response, though an SSRI or SNRI is also accepted as first line., or both
2

Short termacute distress, or severe, disabling symptoms before the antidepressant works

A benzodiazepine, Why short termAdded to an antidepressant, it may speed recovery but does not improve longer-term outcomes; tolerance and dependence are risks; taper it once the antidepressant works.; as a bridge, a slower-onset, longer-acting one such as clonazepam
3

Switchone drug ineffective after at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range

Another SSRI or venlafaxine XR
4

2nd linefirst-line drugs have failed, each after an adequate trial

Clomipramine, imipramine or mirtazapine

In practice:The Canadian guideline lists benzodiazepines as second line. On the exam, use one only as a short-term bridge or add-on, never as long-term treatment on its own.

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Before the first antidepressantAsk about past manic or hypomanic episodesAn antidepressant alone may trigger mania in bipolar disorder
Starting the SSRIFor most, half the usual depression starting dose; raise about every 7 daysEarly activation makes many patients stop it
Acute attack or acute distressA benzodiazepine, short termThen an SSRI with CBT for the long term
Severe symptoms before the SSRI worksA longer-acting benzodiazepine such as clonazepam as a bridgeShort term only; not as the only treatment
History of substance useAn SSRI with CBT; no benzodiazepine bridgeBenzodiazepine misuse and dependence; treat the substance use disorder at the same time
Beta-blocker offered for palpitationsAn SSRI, not propranololPropranolol is not recommended for panic disorder
Buspirone offeredAn SSRI insteadHelps generalized anxiety; does not appear effective for panic disorder
Generalized anxiety disorderCBT, an SSRI or SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), or both; a benzodiazepine Next optionsBuspirone may be considered if the SSRI or SNRI response is inadequate; short-term hydroxyzine or a benzodiazepine for severe symptoms or insomnia while the drug is titrated. Supportive psychotherapy helps but less than CBT. The body symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder should improve when it is treated.Benzodiazepines are less preferred when alcohol is used to self-medicate
Specific phobiaCBT with exposure (systematic desensitization), first lineAn SSRI is first line for panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, not specific phobia; a short-acting benzodiazepine only if therapy is unavailable or refused, or the trigger is rare
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
  1. 2 weeksLittle change at a low dose: raise it
  2. 4 to 6 weeksSome meaningful improvement; judge failure only after 4 weeks at the high end of the range
  3. Several monthsFull effect
  4. 12 months improvedTaper the drug
WhenDo
Little change after 2 weeks at a low doseRaise the dose; not ineffective until at least 4 weeks at the high end of the range
Symptoms improvedContinue the drug for 12 months, then taper, to limit relapse; most have a recurrence even after a symptom-free period
Ongoing careWatch for depression, disability, alcohol and substance use, Also in generalized anxiety disorderGeneralized anxiety disorder also raises the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior: screen, assess risk factors and plan for safety.; ask about agoraphobia, which commonly co-occurs
Practice
  1. 32-year-old woman, 8 months of episodes racing heart, sweating, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; some at rest 7 months avoiding buses, crowds, lines: no escape or help oriented, anxious about the next attack · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, toxicology normal → Panic disorder and agoraphobia → unexpected attacks plus fear of 2 or more situations where escape is hard; when criteria for both are met, both are assigned
  2. 41-year-old man, 9 months of worry, more days than not about job, finances, children's safety; cannot switch it off restless, tired, tense; sleeps poorly No sudden episodes of intense fear alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH normal → Generalized anxiety disorder → excessive worry about a number of events, hard to control, more days than not for at least 6 months, with at least 3 of 6 symptoms; the worry is not about attacks
  3. 23-year-old man, 10 months of pounding heart, sweating, shaking only when presenting in class or eating in the cafeteria fears others will see him blush, think him foolish now skips those classes alert, oriented, euthymic · afebrile; vitals, toxicology normal → Social anxiety disorder → the attacks come only in social situations, and the fear is of negative evaluation, not of the attacks
  4. 27-year-old woman, 1 year of intense fear, sweating, racing heart begins within seconds whenever she must ride an elevator climbs 12 flights of stairs to avoid it No episodes at other times alert, oriented, euthymic · vital signs normal → Specific phobia → one situation almost always provokes immediate fear and is avoided; one situation is not the 2 or more of 5 that agoraphobia needs
  5. 34-year-old woman, 5 months of unexpected spells: choking, nausea, chills, shaking each peaks within minutes and ends; no symptoms between spells dreads the next spell and fears a hidden disease; no drug use HR 74/min · TSH, glucose, ECG, toxicology normal → Panic disorder → unexpected spells that peak within minutes and clear completely, with worry about further attacks, are panic disorder; in somatic symptom disorder the physical symptoms persist over time, and generalized anxiety disorder needs excessive worry about multiple issues, not only about the attacks
  6. 36-year-old woman, 14 months of fear that she has heart disease checks her pulse many times a day has seen three cardiologists No sudden fear episodes; occasional mild chest tightness alert, oriented, anxious, not delusional · afebrile; vitals, ECG, echocardiogram normal → Illness anxiety disorder → persistent preoccupation with a serious illness for at least 6 months with mild or no symptoms; health anxiety in panic disorder is acute and episodic
  7. 29-year-old woman, 3 months of feeling anxious and shaky, with palpitations lost 5 kg (11 lb) without trying feels hot when others are comfortable alert, oriented, restless · HR 112/min · BP 138/70 mm Hg · warm, moist skin · fine hand tremor → Serum TSH → weight loss, heat intolerance and resting tachycardia point to hyperthyroidism; a low TSH screens, and a high free thyroxine confirms
  8. 38-year-old man, 4 months of spells pounding headache, drenching sweats, racing heart each lasts 15 to 30 minutes Alert, oriented, euthymic BP 196/112 mm Hg in a spell, 150/94 between · HR 104/min · TSH 2.1 μU/mL · glucose 96 mg/dL → Plasma free metanephrines → episodes of severe hypertension with headache, sweating and a racing heart point to pheochromocytoma
  9. 22-year-old man, 2 months of sudden episodes racing heart, lightheadedness and fear they start and stop abruptly Alert, oriented, euthymic HR 76/min and BP 122/78 mm Hg between episodes · TSH, glucose and urine toxicology normal → Electrocardiogram → palpitations call for an ECG to look for preexcitation before the episodes are called panic attacks
  10. 26-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; 3 months worrying about the next attack wants a diagnostic test oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, ECG, toxicology normal → Sertraline at a low starting dose and CBT → criteria are met and the mimics are excluded; no test makes the diagnosis, and a lactate challenge has no standardized criteria
  11. 34-year-old man, 6 months of recurrent unexpected episodes intense fear with sweating, palpitations, dizziness, trembling stopped driving 5 months ago, fearing another asks for something to stop them alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → Escitalopram, started low and titrated → an SSRI is first line; a benzodiazepine is for short-term use only, not long-term treatment on its own, and propranolol is not recommended
  12. 28-year-old woman, 5 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, chest pain, fear of losing control months of worry started sertraline 50 mg daily 5 days ago now jittery, more anxious; wants to stop oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 88/min → Lower the dose, then raise it slowly → initial activation can be troubling; start at half the usual depression dose and increase about every 7 days
  13. 31-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying months of worry sertraline 25 mg daily for 2 weeks: little change No adverse effects alert, oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 78/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Raise the sertraline dose → a drug is not ineffective until it has been given for at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range
  14. 25-year-old man, 2 months of unexpected fear episodes palpitations, choking, sweating, chest pain; many a day housebound 6 weeks; cannot work started sertraline yesterday No substance use history oriented · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → A benzodiazepine for the first weeks → with severe symptoms, a longer-acting benzodiazepine such as clonazepam bridges until the antidepressant takes effect; short term only
  15. 40-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, abstinent 2 months 5 months of recurrent unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying avoids leaving home alone alert, oriented, euthymic · vitals, TSH, ECG normal · urine toxicology negative → Alprazolam → benzodiazepines are avoided with a history of substance use because of misuse and dependence; an SSRI with CBT remains first line
  16. 33-year-old woman treated with sertraline and CBT for recurrent unexpected episodes of fear no episodes for 3 months asks to stop the drug alert, euthymic · HR 70/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Continue it for 12 months, then taper → once symptoms improve, continue the drug for 12 months before tapering to limit relapse
Pairs with Bipolar Disorder: any past episode of elevated mood before the antidepressant starts?
Transferable rule

Exclude a substance and a medical cause first. Then name what the fear is about: the attacks themselves, negative evaluation, one object or situation, difficult escape, a number of events, or a serious illness.
